The heavenly sanctuary
Christ as high priest
Blood that cleanses
Heavenly Jerusalem and Mount Zion
A city with foundations
The final shaking of heaven and earth

Hebrews is not a source Revelation alludes to, but the two books share a strikingly similar picture of worship in heaven: a true sanctuary on which the earthly tabernacle was modelled, with its ark, altar and incense, and a heavenly Mount Zion and Jerusalem filled with angels and the redeemed. Both portray Christ's blood as cleansing his people and look for a coming city 'whose designer and builder is God'. Reading them together helps explain why Revelation's throne room is full of temple furniture. Interpreters differ on whether the heavenly temple and city are present spiritual realities, a coming physical city, or both.
True tent in heaven
The earthly tabernacle was a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary 'that the Lord set up'; John sees 'the sanctuary of the tent of witness in heaven' opened.
Ark of the covenant
Hebrews describes the ark and golden altar of incense in the earthly tabernacle; in Revelation God's temple in heaven is opened and the ark of his covenant is seen.
High priest
Jesus is the great high priest who has passed through the heavens; John sees him in a long robe with a golden sash, garments many read as priestly, walking among the lampstands.
Cleansing blood
Christ entered once for all by his own blood, which purifies the conscience; the multitude have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
Mount Zion and the heavenly city

Believers have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, with innumerable angels and the firstborn enrolled in heaven; the Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000 who bear his name, and heaven's myriads worship (5:11).
City with foundations
Abraham looked for the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God (also 11:16 and 13:14); the new Jerusalem comes down from God with twelve foundations bearing the apostles' names.
Shaking heaven and earth
Quoting Haggai 2:6, God will shake heaven and earth once more so that what cannot be shaken may remain; at the great white throne earth and sky flee away, and later a new heaven and earth appear.

Revelation is not a random string of visions. It is carefully built, with numbered sevens, repeated scenes, an opening and closing that mirror each other, and whole sequences borrowed from earlier prophets. Many scholars also think the book is arranged concentrically, so that its first and last parts answer each other and the weight falls in the middle. This study sets out several of those proposals, the verbal bookends that frame the book, similar structures in the Old Testament prophets, and the earlier sequences John follows, while being clear that structural outlines are scholarly proposals rather than settled facts.

A chiasm, or concentric ring composition, arranges material in a mirror pattern, A B C B′ A′, so that the second half retraces the first in reverse order and the centre stands out as the turning point. Ancient texts were mostly heard rather than read silently, and patterns like this helped speakers remember long material and helped listeners follow it, signalling where a section began, where it turned and where it ended. Because the pattern folds back on itself, the centre often carries the main point. A well-known example is Gordon Wenham's argument that the Genesis flood narrative mirrors itself around 8:1, 'God remembered Noah': the waters rise, the ark floats, then the waters fall in reverse order. Scholars debate how many such structures were intended by the authors, but the technique itself is well attested in the Hebrew Bible and the ancient world.
Seven-part concentric outline
Prologue and epistolary greeting
Inaugural vision and the messages to the seven churches
The sealed scroll: seals and trumpets
The small prophetic scroll: the community in conflict with the powers
Bowls and the judgment of Babylon
Parousia, final judgment and the New Jerusalem
Epilogue and epistolary conclusion

Schüssler Fiorenza argues that the book is woven like a tapestry, with interlocking sections rather than simple blocks, so C and C′ overlap and interrupt the centre (C includes 11:15–19, and C′ begins at 15:1 and resumes at 15:5). For drawing the arches the chapter spans here are simplified to C 4–9 and C′ 15–19. On her reading the centre, the small scroll of chapters 10–15, holds the prophetic heart of the book: the conflict between the community and the dragon and beasts.
Historical and eschatological halves in inverse order
Prologue
The church militant: the seven churches
God's work for salvation in progress: throne room and seals
Forces opposing God's people warned and battling: trumpets, dragon and beasts
Forces opposing God's people punished and judged: bowls and Babylon
God's work for salvation completed: heavenly praise, rider, millennium, new creation
The church triumphant: the New Jerusalem
Epilogue

This follows the outline Strand published in 1976–1977, which he called tentative. It has no single central section: the hinge is the line between chapters 14 and 15, where the historical half (evil powers opposing God's people) turns into the eschatological half (evil powers judged), so the two innermost sections D and D′ together form the centre and D is marked here only for drawing. Strand later refined the scheme into eight basic visions, four historical and four eschatological, paired in inverse order between prologue and epilogue (1987); the exact boundaries vary slightly between his versions.
Prologue, two halves and the chapter 12 pivot
First cycle: churches, the sealed scroll, seals and trumpets
The woman, the child and the dragon: the central drama
Second cycle: beasts, bowls, Babylon, the return of Christ and the new creation

Collins divides the body of the book into two great cycles, the second opening at 12:1, and many commentators observe that chapter 12 starts afresh, going back to the birth of the Messiah and exposing the dragon behind the beasts that follow. Treating chapter 12 as a free-standing centre is a simplification of that observation rather than Collins's own diagram, and the boundaries here are approximate.
God gave the revelation to show his servants what must soon take place, sent through his angel to John.
God sent his angel to show his servants what must soon take place.
The same chain of revelation (God, Christ, angel, John, servants) opens and closes the book, with almost identical wording.
Blessed is the one who reads and those who hear and keep what is written in this prophecy.
Blessed is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.
The first and last of the book's seven beatitudes both bless those who keep the prophecy, framing everything between as words to obey, not only to decode.
For the time is near.
Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.
The urgency is identical at both ends. Contrast Daniel 12:4, where Daniel is told to seal the book until the time of the end.
Look, he is coming with the clouds.
Surely I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!
The coming of Christ is announced at the start and promised three times at the close (22:7, 12, 20), ending with the church's answering prayer.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, says the Lord God.
I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.
At the start the title belongs to the Lord God; at the end Jesus speaks it of himself, one of the book's strongest statements of his divine identity.
His servant John; John to the seven churches; I, John, your brother.
I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things.
The prophet names himself as witness at both ends, underlining that the book is testimony he received, not his own invention.
Grace to you and peace; the message to be sent to the seven churches.
I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things for the churches. The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all.
The book is framed as a letter, with an opening grace greeting and a closing grace benediction addressed to the churches.
He has made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father.
His servants will worship him, see his face, and reign for ever and ever.
The priestly kingdom announced at the start (echoing Exodus 19:6) is shown fully realised at the end, as worshippers who see God's face and reign.
Chiasms can be found in almost any long text if a reader looks hard enough and chooses the labels; the pattern may come from the interpreter rather than the author.

This is a real danger, and the variety of proposed outlines shows it. Proposals are more persuasive when they rest on repeated wording and clear markers in the text (as with the bookends of chapters 1 and 22, or the trumpet–bowl parallels) rather than only on broad themes. Even then they remain proposals to be tested, not facts.

Scholars do not agree on where the sections of Revelation begin and end, or on what stands at the centre (chapter 10–15 for Schüssler Fiorenza, the chapter 14–15 hinge for Strand, chapter 12 for others).

The disagreement is genuine. Yet most outlines agree on several points: the prologue and epilogue mirror each other, the seals, trumpets and bowls form a related series, and chapters 12–14 mark a major turn in the book. Readers can hold the shared points with more confidence than any one detailed scheme.
Revelation is plainly organised by numbered sevens and by repeated, overlapping visions (recapitulation), so forcing it into a single mirror pattern may hide its forward movement.

Many scholars see several structuring devices working at once: linear sevens that build to a climax, recapitulating cycles, interlocking transitions and concentric framing. A concentric reading need not replace the others; at its best it highlights the centre and the frame while the sevens carry the story forward.
Daniel 2–7 (the Aramaic chapters)

Adolphe Lenglet (1972), followed by Joyce Baldwin and many others, argued that the Aramaic chapters of Daniel form a concentric unit. Chapters 2 and 7 both portray four world kingdoms replaced by God's kingdom; chapters 3 and 6 both tell of faithful Jews delivered from death (the furnace and the lions' den); chapters 4 and 5 both show God judging a proud king. There is no single middle chapter, so the paired chapters 4–5 are shown here as one central segment: together they make the point that the Most High rules the kingdoms of men (4:17, 25; 5:21).
Four kingdoms: the statue, ended by God's kingdom
Deliverance from the fiery furnace
Judgment on proud kings: Nebuchadnezzar humbled, Belshazzar weighed
Deliverance from the lions' den
Four kingdoms: the four beasts, ended by the Son of Man

Revelation draws heavily on this block. The beast of Revelation 13 combines Daniel 7's four beasts, the demand to worship the image (13:15) recalls Daniel 3, the fall of Babylon (Revelation 17–18) echoes Belshazzar's night in Daniel 5, and the centre's message, that God rules over earthly kingdoms, is the confession of Revelation 11:15.
Zechariah 1:7–6:15 (the night visions)

Joyce Baldwin, Carol and Eric Meyers, and David Dorsey are among those who see the night visions arranged symmetrically. The first and last visions (horses patrolling the earth, chariots going out to the earth) frame the series; the inner visions deal with judgment on the nations and the cleansing of the land; and the centre is the vision of the golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, the two anointed leaders, Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua (chapter 4, with the closely related Joshua scene of chapter 3). Scholars count and pair the visions slightly differently, so the boundaries here are approximate.
Horsemen patrolling the whole earth
Horns and craftsmen; the man with the measuring line
Joshua cleansed; the lampstand and the two olive trees
The flying scroll; the woman in the basket
Four chariots going out to the whole earth

Revelation 11:4 identifies the two witnesses as 'the two olive trees and the two lampstands', taking the centre of Zechariah's visions as the key to the church's prophetic witness. The coloured horses (Zechariah 1:8; 6:2–3) shape the riders of Revelation 6, the measuring line (2:1–2) lies behind Revelation 11:1 and 21:15, and the seven eyes of the LORD (4:10) become the seven eyes of the Lamb (Revelation 5:6).

John Oswalt, among others, sets out the last section of Isaiah as a concentric arrangement. Foreigners gathered to worship (56:1–8) is matched by the nations gathered to see God's glory (66:18–24); Israel's sin and lament (56:9–59:15a) by a further lament and God's answer (63:7–66:17); the LORD as divine warrior (59:15b–21) by the warrior coming from Edom with garments stained red (63:1–6). At the apex stand chapters 60–62: Zion glorified, filled with light, and the Spirit-anointed messenger who proclaims good news. Some scholars divide the outer sections differently, but the central position of 60–62 is widely accepted.
Foreigners and outcasts gathered to worship
Israel's failure, sin and lament
The LORD arms himself as warrior and redeemer
Zion glorified and the anointed messenger
The warrior returns from Edom, robes stained red
Lament, God's answer, new heavens and new earth
The nations gathered to see God's glory

The centre of this structure supplies much of Revelation's New Jerusalem: the glory of God as its light with no need of sun or moon (Isaiah 60:19 → Revelation 21:23), gates never shut and kings bringing their glory into it (60:3, 11 → 21:24–26), and the bride adorned (61:10; 62:5 → 21:2). The flanking warrior of 63:1–6 becomes the rider whose robe is dipped in blood and who treads the winepress (Revelation 19:13–15), and 65:17 and 66:22 give 'a new heaven and a new earth' (21:1).

Jan de Waard (1977) argued that this lament over Israel is a carefully built chiasm, and many later commentators have adopted his outline. A funeral lament (5:1–3) matches wailing in every street (5:16–17); 'seek me and live' (5:4–6) matches 'seek good and not evil, that you may live' (5:14–15); justice turned to wormwood (5:7) matches the abuse of justice in the gate (5:10–13). At the centre stands a hymn to the Creator who made the Pleiades and Orion, turns darkness into morning and brings sudden destruction: 'the LORD is his name' (5:8–9). The whole structure lies within chapter 5, so every segment is drawn at chapter 5 and the verse ranges carry the detail.
Lament: fallen is virgin Israel
Seek me and live
Justice turned to wormwood
The Creator who judges: the LORD is his name
Justice trampled in the gate
Seek good, that you may live
Wailing in all the streets

Revelation shares the same move: judgment on injustice is grounded in the sovereignty of the Creator. The 'Lord God Almighty' of Revelation (4:8; 11:17) echoes Amos's 'LORD God of hosts', rendered 'Almighty' (pantokrator) in the Greek Old Testament; the bitter star named Wormwood (Revelation 8:11) draws on the wormwood image (Amos 5:7; Jeremiah 9:15); and the darkening of the day (Amos 5:8, 18–20) anticipates the darkness of the trumpets and bowls (Revelation 8:12; 16:10).
Joel 1–3 (Hebrew 1–4)

Duane Garrett (1985) and other commentators argue that Joel is a unified composition that turns at 2:18, 'Then the LORD became jealous for his land', with the second half answering the first. The ruined land (chapter 1) is answered by the land restored and 'the years the locust has eaten' repaid (2:18–27); the invading army of the day of the LORD (2:1–11) is answered by the outpouring of the Spirit and judgment on the nations (2:28–3:21). The call to return to the LORD (2:12–17) stands at the turn. This is better described as a symmetrical structure than a strict chiasm, and proposals for Joel vary considerably, so the outline is approximate.
The locust plague ruins the land
The army of the day of the LORD invades
Return to me with all your heart
The LORD pities his land and restores it
The Spirit poured out and the nations judged

Joel supplies Revelation's demonic locusts with lions' teeth, looking like horses prepared for battle and sounding like chariots (Joel 1:6; 2:4–5 → Revelation 9:7–9), the darkened sun and blood-red moon (Joel 2:10, 31 → Revelation 6:12), the question 'who can endure it?' (Joel 2:11 → Revelation 6:17), and the harvest and winepress of the nations (Joel 3:13 → Revelation 14:15–20). Like Joel, Revelation calls for repentance in the face of these judgments (9:20–21).

Ezekiel is usually divided into judgment on Jerusalem (1–24), oracles against the nations (25–32) and restoration (33–48). Commentators such as Daniel Block note that the book is framed by the glory of God: Ezekiel sees it by the Chebar canal (chapter 1), watches it leave the defiled temple (chapters 10–11), and sees it return to the new temple (43:1–5), where he explicitly compares the vision to the earlier ones (43:3). This gives the book a symmetrical frame around the oracles against the nations, though it is a frame rather than a detailed verse-by-verse chiasm.
The glory appears by the Chebar canal; the prophet's commission
Judgment on Jerusalem; the glory departs from the temple
Oracles against the nations
Restoration of Israel: new heart, dry bones, Gog defeated
The new temple; the glory returns

Revelation follows Ezekiel's arc closely: it opens with a throne vision (Revelation 4, from Ezekiel 1) and closes with a measured holy city where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21–22, from Ezekiel 40–48). The final words of Ezekiel, 'The LORD is there' (48:35), become 'the dwelling place of God is with man' (Revelation 21:3). See also the Ezekiel sequence below.
Following Ezekiel's order

Albert Vanhoye (1962) and later Greg Beale and others observed that Revelation does not only quote Ezekiel; it moves through Ezekiel's visions in broadly the same order, from the throne vision at the start to the temple-city at the end. The match is not exact (the supper of the birds, for example, comes before Gog and Magog in Revelation but after it in Ezekiel), yet the overall sequence is striking.
Throne vision: living creatures, rainbow, sea-like expanse
The throne room of heaven
Four living creatures, a rainbow, an expanse like crystal and a figure on the throne appear in both.
The prophet eats a scroll, sweet as honey
John eats the little scroll
In both the scroll is sweet in the mouth, and in Revelation bitter in the stomach, before the prophet is sent to prophesy again.
A mark on the foreheads of those who grieve
The servants of God sealed on their foreheads
The faithful are marked for protection before judgment falls.
Burning coals from among the cherubim scattered over the city
Fire from the altar thrown on the earth
Fire from God's presence becomes the signal for judgment.
Jerusalem and Samaria as unfaithful prostitutes
The great prostitute, Babylon
Both use the image of a harlot city stripped and burned by her former lovers (Ezekiel 16:37–41; 23:25–29; Revelation 17:16).
Lament over Tyre, the merchant city
Lament over fallen Babylon
Kings, merchants and seafarers mourn, and the cargo list of Ezekiel 27 is echoed in Revelation 18:11–19.
The valley of dry bones comes to life
The first resurrection; the saints live and reign
Beale and others see the revival of God's people in Ezekiel 37 behind the coming to life in Revelation 20, before the Gog battle in both books.
Gog of the land of Magog attacks and is destroyed
Gog and Magog gathered for battle and consumed by fire
Revelation names Gog and Magog directly, and fire from heaven ends the attack in both (Ezekiel 38:22; 39:6).
Birds summoned to a sacrificial feast
The great supper of God
The invitation to the birds to eat the flesh of kings and mighty men is closely reproduced.
The measured temple, the city and the river of life
The measured New Jerusalem and the river of the water of life
Measuring (Ezekiel 40:3; Revelation 21:15), twelve gates named for the tribes (48:31–34; 21:12), and a river with fruit trees whose leaves heal (47:1–12; 22:1–2).
The Exodus plagues in the trumpets and bowls

The trumpets and bowls are modelled on the plagues of Egypt, and the people of God are pictured as a new Israel delivered through judgment and singing by the sea. Most commentators note this pattern, including Bauckham and Beale, though Revelation rearranges and intensifies the plagues rather than copying them in order.
Sea and rivers become blood
The first Egyptian plague returns in the second trumpet and the second and third bowls.
Frogs
Three unclean spirits like frogs
The frogs become deceiving spirits from the dragon, beast and false prophet.
Boils on people and animals
Painful sores on the beast's worshippers
The first bowl repeats the sixth plague.
Hail mixed with fire; huge hailstones
The first trumpet and the seventh bowl both recall the seventh plague.
Locusts cover the land
The locusts become a demonic army that torments people rather than crops.
Darkness over Egypt
Sun, moon and stars darkened; the beast's kingdom plunged into darkness
As in Egypt, darkness falls on the oppressor's realm.
The Passover lamb whose blood protects
The Lamb who was slain ransoms a people
The Lamb's blood redeems and protects, making a new people out of every nation.
The song of Moses beside the sea
The song of Moses and of the Lamb beside the sea of glass
The conquerors stand by the sea and sing of God's righteous deeds, as Israel did after crossing the Red Sea.
Daniel 7 in Revelation 13 and 17

Daniel 7 is one of the most important sources for Revelation. John takes its vision of beasts from the sea, the arrogant horn, the heavenly court and the kingdom given to the saints, and reworks it in Revelation 13, 17 and 20. Beale has argued that Daniel is the dominant Old Testament background of the whole book.
Four great beasts rise from the stirred-up sea
A beast rises out of the sea
The setting of the sea, a symbol of chaos and the nations, is the same.
Lion, bear and leopard
One beast like a leopard, with feet like a bear's and a mouth like a lion's
Daniel's successive beasts are merged into one, in reverse order, suggesting a power that sums up all the empires.
The fourth beast with ten horns
Ten horns, explained as ten kings
Both John and Daniel explain the horns as kings who rule with the beast.
A horn with a mouth speaking great things against the Most High
A mouth uttering great and blasphemous things
The blasphemous speech of the little horn passes to the beast.
The horn makes war on the saints for a time, times and half a time
War on the saints for forty-two months; time, times and half a time
The same limited period of persecution is used in several forms (3½ years, 42 months, 1,260 days).
Thrones set, the Ancient of Days seated, books opened
Thrones, the great white throne, books opened
The heavenly court scene becomes the final judgment.
The beast slain and given over to burning fire
The beast thrown alive into the lake of fire
The fate of the beast is the same.
One like a son of man; dominion given to the saints
The Son of Man coming with the clouds; the saints reign
The kingdom is given to the Son of Man and shared with his people.
Genesis 1–3 reversed in Revelation 21–22

The Bible's last two chapters answer its first three. Creation, Eden and the curse are taken up again, but now the curse is lifted, the serpent is defeated and God dwells openly with his people. Many writers, including Beale and Middleton, read the New Jerusalem as Eden restored and enlarged into a temple-city filling the new creation.
God creates the heavens and the earth
A new heaven and a new earth; 'I am making all things new'
The story ends where it began, with creation renewed rather than abandoned.
The deep and the seas
The sea is no more
The sea, an image of chaos and the source of the beast (13:1), has no place in the new creation.
Light, sun and moon
No need of sun or moon; the Lord God is their light
Created lights give way to the direct light of God's glory.
A river flows out of Eden; gold and precious stones
The river of the water of life; a city of gold and jewels
Eden's river and treasures reappear in the city.
The tree of life, then barred by cherubim
The tree of life open to those who wash their robes
Access lost in Genesis is restored.
Pain, toil and death
No more death, mourning, crying or pain
The effects of the fall are undone.
The ground cursed
No longer will there be anything accursed
The curse is removed at the end.
The serpent deceives; its head to be crushed
The ancient serpent, the devil, bound and thrown into the lake of fire
The promise of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled.
God walking in the garden; the humans hide
God dwells with his people; they will see his face
Hiding from God gives way to open, face-to-face fellowship.

Revelation is full of places: Babylon, Sodom and Egypt, Mount Zion, the Euphrates, Armageddon and seven real cities in Roman Asia. This atlas maps the places behind its imagery across the whole biblical story, so you can see how John's visions draw on the geography of earlier Scripture and of his own world. Where a site's location or a date is uncertain, the notes say so.
Patriarchs and Exodus

Abraham leaves Mesopotamia on the strength of God's promise, and his descendants go down to Egypt and are brought out through plagues, Passover and the sea. At Sinai God makes them a kingdom of priests, a pattern Revelation repeatedly echoes.
Kingdom and prophets

David and Solomon establish Jerusalem and its temple, and the prophets confront kings and announce judgement on Israel and the nations. Assyria and then Babylon rise as the great powers whose fall the prophets foretell.
Exile and return

Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple, and prophets such as Ezekiel and Daniel receive visions among the exiles. Under Persia some return to rebuild the city and temple, while others stay in the eastern diaspora.
Greek and Maccabean age

Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture, and his successors in Egypt and Syria fight over the land of Israel. The persecution under Antiochus IV and the Maccabean revolt shape later readings of Daniel's beasts and times.
Rome and the first churches
63 BC-AD 70

Pompey brings Judea under Roman control, Jesus is crucified under Pontius Pilate, and the gospel spreads from Jerusalem through Antioch to Asia and Rome. The era closes with Nero's persecution and the destruction of Jerusalem's temple in AD 70.
John on Patmos

John receives Revelation in exile on Patmos and writes to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia. Scholars debate the date: an early date under Nero or soon after (c. AD 68-69) and a late date under Domitian (c. AD 95, following Irenaeus) are both defended, with the late date the majority view.
Eden (traditional location)

Genesis places the garden where God put the first humans at the source of four rivers, two of which are the Tigris and the Euphrates. There the serpent deceived the woman and the way to the tree of life was closed.
Revelation ends where Genesis began: the ancient serpent is defeated, and the tree of life and a river stand again in the city of God, with no more curse.

The real location of Eden is unknown, and Genesis may not intend a mappable site at all. This marker follows one traditional guess near the meeting of the Tigris and Euphrates in southern Iraq; others have suggested Armenia or elsewhere.
Ur of the Chaldeans
Abram's family set out from Ur of the Chaldeans on the long journey that began the story of God's covenant people.
Revelation does not name Ur, but its picture of a people called out of Babylon's land to a city with foundations echoes Abraham, who left Mesopotamia looking for the city whose builder is God.
Most scholars identify biblical Ur with Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq, excavated by Leonard Woolley, though a minority have proposed a northern Ur near Haran.
Haran
Terah's family settled in Haran, and from there Abram obeyed God's call to go to the land he would be shown. Jacob later fled to Haran and married there.
Haran is not named in Revelation; it marks the start of the promise to bless all the families of the earth, which Revelation sees fulfilled in a people from every tribe and nation.
Haran, in modern south-east Turkey, was a long-lived trading city and a centre of the moon god Sin, the same deity honoured at Ur.
Egypt (Memphis)
Israel went down to Egypt in Joseph's day, was enslaved, and was set free when God struck Egypt with plagues and the Passover lamb was slain.
Revelation's trumpets and bowls echo the plagues on Egypt, the redeemed sing the song of Moses, and the great city is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt.
Memphis, near modern Cairo, was the old capital of Lower Egypt. The date of the Exodus is debated, with an earlier date around 1446 BC and a later one around 1260 BC both defended.
Mount Sinai (traditional Jebel Musa)
At Sinai God came down in fire, cloud, thunder and a trumpet blast, gave the law, and made Israel a kingdom of priests.
Revelation's lightning, voices and thunder before the throne recall Sinai, and the redeemed are made a kingdom and priests to God, as Israel was at Sinai.

The location of Sinai is uncertain. Jebel Musa in southern Sinai is the traditional site, honoured since the fourth century, but scholars have also proposed sites in northern Sinai and in north-west Arabia.
Sodom (south of the Dead Sea, uncertain)
Lot settled near Sodom, and God destroyed the cities of the plain with fire and sulfur from heaven because of their wickedness.
Revelation calls the great city where the Lord was crucified spiritually Sodom, and its lake of fire and sulfur draws on Sodom's judgement.

The site is not known. A traditional view places Sodom near the southern end of the Dead Sea, while some archaeologists argue for Tall el-Hammam north-east of the Dead Sea; both proposals are disputed.
Jericho
After the Exodus Israel crossed the Jordan and marched around Jericho for seven days, with seven priests blowing seven trumpets, until the walls fell.
Revelation's seven trumpets, sounding before the fall of a hostile city and the coming of the kingdom, echo the pattern of Jericho.
Tell es-Sultan is one of the oldest continuously settled sites known. The dating of its destruction layers and their relation to Joshua remain debated among archaeologists.
